The positive imperative for “tú” is EXACTLY the “él / ella” form of the present. No change at all!
For “vosotros” it’s even simpler: change the -r of the infinitive to -d: hablar → ¡Hablad!, comer → ¡Comed!, venir → ¡Venid!

4. Pronouns are attached at the end
In the POSITIVE imperative, the pronouns are attached to the end of the verb, a bit like English “give-me-it” written as one word: “dámelo”.
Don’t forget the written accent when you attach pronouns to a verb of 2+ syllables: corta + las = córtalas.
The NEGATIVE imperative (“don’t do it!”) has a different form: “no llores”, “no lo hagas”. We study it in detail in the next chapter.

The recipe for the cold summer soup from Andalusia, written politely, as in a cookbook.
Gazpacho is a cold vegetable soup. It’s perfect for very hot days.
Ingredients for four people: a kilo of ripe tomatoes, a cucumber and a green pepper.
You will also need a clove of garlic, day-old bread, olive oil, vinegar and salt.
First, wash all the vegetables well.
Cut the tomatoes, the cucumber and the pepper into large pieces.
Soak the bread in water for five minutes.
Then put everything in the blender with the garlic and blend very well.
Add the oil little by little, a little vinegar and salt to taste.
If you want a smoother gazpacho, pass it through a sieve.
Put it in the fridge for at least two hours. It must be very cold.
Serve it in glasses or bowls, with small pieces of cucumber and croutons.
One Saturday, while she was cleaning her grandmother’s house, Ana found an old notebook in a kitchen drawer.
The pages were yellow and the handwriting was small and elegant. It was the recipe notebook of her great-grandmother, Rosario’s mother.
The first recipe was for the famous cocido. Ana read it out loud:
“Put the chickpeas to soak the night before. Don’t forget, or they’ll be as hard as stone.”
“In the morning, put water in a big pot and add the meat, the chorizo and the bacon. Simmer over a low heat for three hours.”
“Don’t rush. Cocido is like love: it needs time.”
Ana smiled. She read on and found recipes for croquettes, flan, doughnuts…
At the end of each recipe, her great-grandmother had written a piece of life advice.
Under the flan recipe it said: “Don’t add too much sugar. Things that are too sweet soon tire you.”
Under the croquettes: “Make plenty, because someone always turns up unannounced. And always share what you have.”
And on the last page: “If something goes wrong, don’t cry. Laugh, clean the kitchen and start again.”
When Rosario came back from the market, Ana showed her the notebook. Grandma took it in both hands, like a treasure.
“I’ve been looking for it for years,” she said quietly. “My mother cooked from this notebook every day.”
That afternoon they cooked her great-grandmother’s doughnuts together, following the recipe step by step.
They came out a bit ugly, but they were delicious. And, as the notebook said, they laughed, cleaned the kitchen… and made some more.
Since that day the notebook has stayed in Rosario’s kitchen, by the window. Every Sunday Ana copies a new recipe into her phone so it’s never lost again.
